title: A population difference arriving as inconsistency
question: When the studies supplying the direct and indirect paths of a loop differ in an effect modifier, how often does unadjusted node splitting flag the population difference as inconsistency or miss a real conflict that the difference cancels, and what does an adjusted split achieve?
design: Triangle networks with a covariate gap between the direct and indirect study sets, modification strength, true loop inconsistency and two or four studies per comparison; unadjusted and meta-regression-adjusted node splits. 54 cells, 2000 replicates each.
answer: Unadjusted node splitting tests inconsistency plus population mismatch. With no true inconsistency it flagged 14% to 98% of analyses when the direct and indirect study sets differed in an effect modifier, and it fell to its null rate when the mismatch cancelled a real conflict. A split adjusted for the modifier held size (4% to 6%) and recovered some masked conflicts, but its precision fell as the gap between the study sets grew.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: unadjusted flag rate 0.141 to 0.982 with no inconsistency and differing populations; adjusted 0.041 to 0.058.
Exact masking: unadjusted 0.058 to 0.105; adjusted 0.074 to 0.254.
Adjusted inconsistency SE rose from 0.10 to 0.30 as the covariate gap went from 0 to 1 (four studies per comparison, modification 0.4); power against 0.2 fell from 0.54 to 0.12.
Unadjusted split at 0.10 even with no gap under modification 0.4, from covariate-driven heterogeneity.
not_answered: Continuous study estimates, one loop, no Bayesian node split or marginalization to a named target. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Loop inconsistency factor for the B versus C contrast
